Garden
gär'dn
n. (an enclosed cultivated ground; rendering Hebrew gan, Greek kepos)
From the Old French jardin, of Germanic origin, akin to yard and to gird — the root idea is an enclosure. Hebrew gan is likewise from ganan, to enclose or defend, so a garden in Scripture is fenced ground, cultivated and protected.

Biblical Definition

Garden frames the whole Bible. It opens in one: “the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed” (Genesis 2:8) — man's first estate is cultivated ground with work to do in it, which dignifies labour before the fall and forbids the notion that work is a curse. Sin drives him out, and an angel with a flaming sword keeps the way. The great reversal begins in another garden, for it was over the brook Cedron that our Lord went “where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples” (John 18:1) — where the first Adam failed under no pressure at all, the last Adam obeyed under the sweat of blood. And the burial is in a third: “in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre” (John 19:41), so that Mary, meeting him risen, supposed him to be the gardener — a mistake that was in a deeper sense no mistake. The garden also figures the soul kept and watered by God: “thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not” (Isaiah 58:11); and the bride is “a garden inclosed… a spring shut up, a fountain sealed” (Song of Solomon 4:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Enclosed, cultivated ground. Scripture begins in a garden, is redeemed through two more — Gethsemane and the sepulchre's — and pictures the well-tended soul as a watered garden.

expand to see more

GARDEN, n. [Fr. jardin; allied to yard, an enclosure.] A piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, fruits, flowers or plants.

2. A rich, well cultivated spot or tract of country; as, the garden of the world.

3. Figuratively, a place of delight or of careful keeping.

4. In Scripture, the garden of Eden, in which God placed the man he had formed, Gen. 2.

5. Of the soul under God's care; as, thou shalt be like a watered garden, Isa. 58.

Key Scripture

Genesis 2:8 — "And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed."

John 18:1 — "When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples."

John 19:41 — "Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid."

Isaiah 58:11 — "And the LORD shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not."

Modern Corruption

Eden is treated as myth and work as a consequence of the fall. Genesis makes the garden a real place with real cultivation given before any sin, so that labour is part of man's original dignity.

expand to see more

Reading Eden as symbol rather than history costs more than a chapter. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 rests on a historical Adam whose one act brought death upon all, and the parallel collapses if the first Adam is a figure and the last is a man. The dictionary holds to a historical Adam and Eve and a real garden, with the genealogies of Genesis 5 and Luke 3 treating Adam as an ancestor rather than an archetype.

The second recovery concerns work. God put the man in the garden to dress it and to keep it before the serpent had spoken a word, so cultivation is not punishment; what the fall added was thorns, thistles, and sweat. That distinction matters for how a Christian regards Monday. And the three gardens together tell the gospel in a line: in the first, a man in a place of ease disobeyed and was driven out; in Gethsemane, a man in agony obeyed and said not my will, but thine, be done; in the third, the stone was rolled away, and the woman who met him thought he was the gardener.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gan is an enclosed garden, from ganan, to fence or defend; gannah is a garden plot, and Eden means delight. Greek kepos is a garden or orchard, and paradeisos is a park, the Septuagint's word for Eden.

expand to see more

Hebrew gan (H1588) — a garden, an enclosure; the garden eastward in Eden.

Hebrew ganan (H1598) — to enclose, to defend, to protect; the root idea behind the noun.

Hebrew eden (H5731) — delight, pleasure; the region in which the garden was planted.

Greek kepos (G2779) — a garden; Gethsemane and the garden of the sepulchre.

Greek paradeisos (G3857) — a park or paradise; today shalt thou be with me in paradise, Luke 23:43.

Usage

"Of man's first estate: the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden (Genesis 2:8)."

"Of the place of Christ's agony: over the brook Cedron, where was a garden (John 18:1)."

"Of the soul God keeps: thou shalt be like a watered garden (Isaiah 58:11)."
